connector: The novel is finished. Now Lois Lowry steps out from behind it and talks to you herself. She tells you where the facts end and the story begins. Read with this week’s list beside you. Some things you guessed were made up turn out to be true.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, this is Grete. The story is over, and now Lois Lowry steps out from behind it to speak to you herself. She tells you what was real. You’ll warm up, work with words, read the Afterword, and publish your essay. Today’s question: what in this novel actually happened, and what did the Danes really do?
transcripts.wgrd: Get out your list from this week, the one with could be real and made up. As you read the Afterword, check each guess against what Lowry actually says. Mark it real, made up, or still not sure. Then go back to one scene you loved, and read a few lines again, now that you know.
transcripts.dol: The model is a short sentence about the author. The sentence to fix has three sound-alike words, and each one is the wrong twin. One should introduce something, one should be a number, and one should mean it is. It also needs a mark that tells the reader an explanation is coming.
transcripts.guide1: This is the last word work of the book, and it’s a full editing pass. Some sentences are already right. Some carry a wrong twin. Tap only what needs an editor, and leave the rest alone. Remember: your ear is no help here. Your eyes are.
transcripts.morphology: The last four windows. When these words are in place, the whole street will be lit. You’ve met every one of these words before, so this is a chance to show yourself what you know. Shape, or bending? Then look up at the rooftops.
transcripts.vocabulary: One last match. Then use two of these words together, in a sentence about the whole book. Try compare and conclude: put the novel beside the real history, and say what you decide. Your sentence can be about Annemarie, about the real Danes, or about both at once.
transcripts.grammar: These sentences are all about the Afterword. Some are right, and some hide a wrong sound-alike word. Tap every sentence that has a mistake. Then fix one, and explain why reading it out loud would never have caught the problem.
transcripts.spelling: Same idea, word by word this time. Tap only the words that are the wrong twin. Then fix one and say the rule that helped you. If you made up a trick this week for remembering a pair, now is the time to use it.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about ordinary people. My mother was not a hero in any book. She kept a neighbor family’s spare key in her sewing box for two years, and watered their plants until they came home. Lowry tells you Annemarie is made up. But people like my mother were real, all over Denmark. Read for them.
transcripts.read: Read the Afterword slowly. Lowry talks to you directly here, one writer to one reader. She names what she made up and what really happened, and some of the true parts may surprise you. At the very end, she shares a letter from a real young man. Read his words twice.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. Name one thing Lowry says is real and one thing she made up, using her own words. Then think about her friend who grew up in Copenhagen, and what that tells you about historical fiction. Last, set your essay’s claim beside what Lowry says about the Danish people, and publish.
transcripts.chapter: The third question puts your essay next to the real history. Read your claim again, then read what Lowry says about the Danish people. Does your claim still hold? Where does it grow? You don’t have to throw your claim away. You make it deeper.
transcripts.workshop: This is the day you publish. Paste in your whole finished essay. Then write three short sentences: what your claim was, what the real history says, and what putting them side by side taught you. Read it once more, out loud. You wrote an essay from the first idea to the last word.

a.raw: their are too parts to a historical novel a story and the real history its built on
a.fixed: There are two parts to a historical novel: a story and the real history it’s built on.
a.why: There (introduces what exists, not their); two (the number, not too); a colon before the explanation; it’s (it is), not its (belonging); a period at the end.

b.raw: lowry tells us too true things the handkerchief was real and its powder fooled the dogs
b.fixed: Lowry tells us two true things: the handkerchief was real, and its powder fooled the dogs.
b.why: A capital L on Lowry; two (the number, not too); a colon before the explanation; a comma before and; its is right this time (the powder belongs to the handkerchief); a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain which fact surprised you most.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain why a made-up girl still needed a real friend’s memories.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say exactly how your claim grows.

match.conform: Conform has the shape root inside it. Look for the meaning about matching or fitting in.
match.reflect: Reflect has a bending root inside it. Look for the meaning about bending back, or thinking back.
match.compare: Compare is about putting two things side by side. Look for the meaning about what is the same and what is different.
match.conclude: Conclude is about the end. Look for the meaning about finishing, or coming to a final idea.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: a shape, or bending?

why.t: On the evening of May 4, 1945, Danish radio from London told Denmark that the German soldiers there were giving up. For five years, every window had been covered at night so that no light could show. That evening, people tore down the dark curtains, and light shone from the windows again. A few years later, Danes began putting candles in their windows every May 4 to remember, and many still do. form means shape, and flect and flex both mean bend. Each right word lights one window. Four each lesson, until the whole street glows.

miss.fill1: Not quite. Read the meaning again. Is this word about a shape, or about bending?
miss.fill2: Not quite. Read the meaning again. Is this word about a shape, or about bending?
miss.fill3: Not quite. This word is about bending, not a shape. flect and flex both mean bend, so say the word out loud and listen to its ending.
miss.fill4: Not quite. This word is about bending, not a shape. flect and flex both mean bend, so say the word out loud and listen to its ending.

wordgame.win: Every window on the street is lit, and the flags are out. Denmark is free again. form = shape · flect and flex = bend.

notes.wgrd: An author’s note is nonfiction behind the story. Check each guess on your list against what the author actually says: real, made up, or not sure.
vocab: To match a shape or rule; to fit in with something.
To think back; or, to bounce light or an image.
To look at two things and notice what is the same and what is different.
To finish; to come to a final idea.
notes.wordParts: form means “shape,” and flect and flex both mean “to bend”: conform, reform, reflect, flexible.
notes.grammar: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings: their (belonging), there (a place), they’re (they are); to (toward), too (very or also), two (the number).
notes.spelling: Your ear can’t tell homophones apart, so look at each one and ask what it means in that spot. The meaning decides the spelling: to the water, too dangerous, two soldiers.

case.title: The King Rides Alone
case.alt: An older man in uniform rides a dark horse down a busy city street, with people on bicycles all around him.
label: During the occupation, King Christian X rode his horse through the streets of Copenhagen almost every morning, with no guards around him. People on bicycles rode alongside, and some tipped their hats.

In Chapter 2, Papa tells a story about a German soldier who asked a Danish boy who the rider was. In the Afterword, Lois Lowry says that story is true: it is written down in papers that still remain from that time.

look.q: Why might it matter that the king rode out with no guards?
look.a: It showed he was not afraid, and that he still belonged to his people, not to the soldiers.

look.q: What else in the Afterword turned out to be true?
look.a: The sinking of the Danish navy, the warning before the Jewish New Year, the escape of nearly seven thousand people, and the handkerchief.
